blocks.text: Branching on data: if, elif, else

Not every line of code should always run — sometimes what happens next depends on the data. An if statement executes its block only when its condition is true. You can add zero or more elif parts after an if, and an optional else at the end; elif is short for 'else if' and keeps the code flat instead of deeply nested.

steps.title: Visiting every item: the for loop
steps.lede: Process every delivery time in a list without writing the same code over and over.

blocks.text: Visiting every item: the for loop

Once delivery times are collected in a list, you'll want to do something with every single one of them, not just one at a time by hand. Python's for statement iterates over the items of any sequence — such as a list or a string — in the order they appear. Each pass binds the loop variable to the next item:

for minutes in delivery_times:
    print(minutes)

This prints every delivery time in delivery_times, one per pass.

A for loop visits every item of a sequence such as a list once, in the order the items appear, which is what you need to process each delivery time in turn.

remediation_steps.title: When does an if block run?
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit the rule for when an if block executes.

blocks.text: Reminder: when does an if block run?

An if statement executes its block only when its condition is true — not every time the code runs. If delivery_minutes = 30 and the condition is delivery_minutes > 45, the block is skipped entirely. The block runs only when the condition evaluates to True.

remediation_steps.title: Which branch runs in a chain?
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit how an if/elif/else chain selects exactly one branch.

blocks.text: Reminder: which branch runs in a chain?

An if/elif/else chain evaluates conditions one by one from top to bottom. The first condition that is true wins — its block runs and all others are skipped. If no condition is true, the else block (if present) runs. With delivery_minutes = 30: the first condition (< 15) is false, the second (< 45) is true, so category = 'normal' runs and the else branch is skipped.

remediation_steps.title: What value does the loop variable hold?
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit how the loop variable takes each value in turn.

blocks.text: Reminder: what value does the loop variable hold?

Each pass through a for loop binds the loop variable to the next item of the sequence. With delivery_times = [32, 45, 21, 60, 18], the first pass sets minutes = 32, the second sets minutes = 45, and so on. The variable takes each value in order, one per pass.

steps.title: Repeating while a condition holds: the while loop
steps.lede: Keep processing deliveries as long as there are still orders to handle.

blocks.text: Repeating while a condition holds: the while loop

Sometimes you don't know in advance how many times you'll need to repeat something — you just want to keep going as long as some condition holds. A while loop executes its body repeatedly as long as its condition remains true; the condition can be a comparison, such as a < 10.

The body is indented beneath the while line, and something in the body must change what the condition checks — otherwise the loop never stops:

pending = 3
while pending > 0:
    print('deliveries left:', pending)
    pending = pending - 1

Each pass prints the current count and decreases pending by 1, so the loop stops once pending reaches 0.

steps.title: Steering mid-loop: break and continue
steps.lede: Exit a loop early or skip a bad record without stopping the whole loop.

blocks.text: Steering mid-loop: break and continue

The break statement exits the innermost enclosing for or while loop immediately — useful for stopping a search over delivery orders as soon as the one you want is found. The continue statement skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one — for example, skipping a delivery record that's missing a time without exiting the whole loop.

blocks.text: Unlike a for loop, which is bound to a known collection, a while loop keeps running purely based on its condition — so the code inside it must eventually make that condition false or the loop never stops. Use break to exit a loop early and continue to skip the rest of the current iteration.

remediation_steps.title: The body must change what the condition checks
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit why the loop body must update the condition variable.

blocks.text: Reminder: the body must change what the condition checks

The body of a while loop must change what the condition checks — otherwise the condition stays true forever and the loop never stops. In the pending example, pending = pending - 1 decreases pending each pass, so pending > 0 eventually becomes false and the loop exits.

remediation_steps.title: continue vs break
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit the difference between continue and break.

blocks.text: Reminder: continue vs break

continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one — the loop keeps running. break exits the innermost loop entirely — no more iterations happen. Use continue to skip a bad record; use break to stop searching once you've found what you need.

steps.title: Building lists and dicts in one line: comprehensions
steps.lede: Replace multi-line loops with compact, readable expressions.

blocks.text: Building lists and dicts in one line: comprehensions

Building a new list from an existing one by looping is common enough that Python has a shorthand for it. A list comprehension consists of brackets containing an expression followed by a for clause, and optionally one or more for or if clauses; it produces a new list by evaluating the expression for each item — [minutes * 2 for minutes in delivery_times] doubles every value.

Add an if clause to filter the source: [minutes for minutes in delivery_times if minutes >= 45] keeps only the delivery times that satisfy that condition. Dict comprehensions work the same way with curly braces and a key: value expression — {city: len(city) for city in ('Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano')} maps each city name to its length.

after.code:
# Equivalent list comprehension
doubled = [minutes * 2 for minutes in delivery_times if minutes >= 45]

annotations.text: expression · for clause · if clause — all in one line

blocks.change_summary: Five lines collapse to one: the expression, for clause and if clause move inside brackets.

steps.title: Looping over any collection: lists, dicts, sets and tuples
steps.lede: The same for loop syntax works on every collection — what changes is what you get back.

blocks.text: Looping over any collection: lists, dicts, sets and tuples

You've already looped over lists with for. The same for x in ... pattern works on other collections, but what you get back per pass differs. Looping directly over a dictionary yields its keys — for order_id in order_city: visits each order id, not each city. To get both key and value together, use .items(): for order_id, city in order_city.items(): print(order_id, city).

A set's elements may come out in a different order than expected when iterated over, because a set is unordered — looping over a set of cities won't necessarily visit them in the order they were added. Tuples are a sequence type, so a for loop visits their items in order the same way it does for a list — for value in order: visits 1042, then 'Lagos', then 32, when order = (1042, 'Lagos', 32).

blocks.right_label: What the loop variable holds each pass

left.code:
# list
for minutes in delivery_times: ...

# dict (keys only)
for order_id in order_city: ...

# dict (key + value)
for order_id, city in order_city.items(): ...

# set
for city in {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'}: ...

# tuple
for value in (1042, 'Lagos', 32): ...

right.code:
# each integer delivery time in order
# e.g. 32, 45, 21, 60, 18 …

# each integer key
# e.g. 1042, 1043, 1044 …

# each (key, value) pair
# e.g. (1042, 'Lagos'), (1043, 'Abuja') …

# each element — order not guaranteed
# may be 'Kano', 'Lagos', 'Abuja' or any order

# each item in sequence order
# 1042, then 'Lagos', then 32

blocks.takeaway: The for x in ... syntax is the same for every collection; what changes is what each pass hands you.

blocks.text: A comprehension does in one line what a for loop with an if check and an empty list to append into would otherwise take several lines to build. The same for x in ... syntax works across lists, dicts, sets and tuples — what changes is what each pass hands you: an item, a key, or with .items() a key-value pair. For a set, the order isn't guaranteed.

remediation_steps.title: Dict comprehension syntax
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit how to write a dict comprehension.

blocks.text: Reminder: dict comprehension syntax

Dict comprehensions use curly braces with a key: value expression before the for clause — {city: len(city) for city in ('Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano')} maps each city name to its length. The key and value expressions can be any valid Python expression; the result is a new dictionary, not a list.

remediation_steps.title: Sets are unordered
remediation_steps.lede: Let's revisit why set iteration order is not guaranteed.

blocks.text: Reminder: sets are unordered

A set's elements may come out in a different order than expected when iterated over, because a set is unordered. Looping over {'Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'} won't necessarily visit them in the order they were written — the order can vary between runs. If order matters, use a list or tuple instead.
